overview: Pinacosaurus (meaning 'plank lizard') was a medium-sized ankylosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 89–72 million years ago, in what are now the Gobi Desert regions of Mongolia and northern China. Named by Gilmore in 1933, it reached an estimated length of about 5 metres and weighed around 1,000 kg, walking on four sturdy legs covered by bony armour. Fossils are known from formations including the Djadokhta, Bayan Mandahu, and Baruungoyot, across Omnogov and Nei Mongol provinces.

Pinacosaurus is scientifically notable for the discovery of juvenile specimens apparently fossilised together in groups, suggesting some degree of gregarious or herding behaviour in young individuals. It belongs to Ankylosauridae within Ankylosauria, and its Mongolian occurrences have helped palaeontologists understand ankylosaur diversity across the Late Cretaceous of Asia. The genus had small nasal openings with unusual accessory openings, whose function remains debated.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Pinacosaurus was named by Charles W. Gilmore in 1933 based on material collected from Mongolia during the American Museum of Natural History expeditions of the 1920s. The type species is Pinacosaurus grangeri, honouring collector Walter Granger. Additional specimens have since been recovered by Mongolian-Soviet and later Mongolian-Japanese expeditions.

articles.title: Juvenile Aggregations
articles.body: One of the most remarkable features of Pinacosaurus is the discovery of multiple juvenile individuals fossilised together in the same locality, interpreted by some researchers as evidence of herding or social grouping in young dinosaurs. This is relatively unusual in the ankylosaur fossil record and has informed debates about parental care and social behaviour in ornithischians.

articles.title: Anatomy and Armour
articles.body: Pinacosaurus possessed the characteristic ankylosaur body armour of osteoderms embedded in the skin, along with a tail club used for defence. Its skull shows unusual multiple accessory nasal openings flanking the main naris, the function of which—whether related to thermoregulation, olfaction, or display—has not been conclusively determined.

articles.title: Ecological Setting
articles.body: During the Late Cretaceous, the Gobi region was a semi-arid landscape of dunes and ephemeral water sources. Pinacosaurus shared its environment with small theropods, early mammals, and other dinosaurs of the Djadokhta fauna, browsing on low-growing vegetation with its herbivorous diet.

record.description: Pinacosaurus grangeri was an ankylosaurid from Campanian deposits of Mongolia and northern China, represented by numerous skulls and skeletons, especially juvenile groups.
facts: Exceptional juvenile assemblages preserve multiple associated individuals rather than one mass-complete skeleton.
Skulls show characteristic accessory openings near the nostrils, whose soft-tissue function remains debated.
A tail club is supported by ankylosaurid anatomy and referred caudal material, but armour layouts vary with preservation and growth.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure occurrences are Campanian Djadokhta-equivalent deposits; the range is not extended using undiagnostic ankylosaur material.
